decks.title: Computer Systems — Part 1: Organisation, Memory and Software
goals: Describe the components of a computer system and the parts of the CPU
Compare cache, RAM, ROM and secondary memory, and convert between memory units
Classify software as system, utility or application, and tell translators apart
State the main functions of an operating system

slides.heading: Computer Systems and Organisation
slides.body_md: Part 1: how a computer is organised, how memory is measured and what kinds of software run on it.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: the computer system, the CPU, memory and its units, types of software, language translators and the operating system
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Every phone, laptop and ATM is a computer system. In this part we open it up. We look at the CPU, the memories that feed it, how memory is measured in bytes, and the different kinds of software that make the hardware useful, including the operating system that manages it all.

slides.heading: A machine that takes in, works on and keeps data
slides.body_md: A **computer** accepts **input**, **processes** it by following instructions, produces **output**, and can **store** data for later.

nodes.label: Process: the CPU works on them

visual.alt: Flow of the input, process, output and storage cycle: data and instructions go in, the CPU processes them, results come out, and data can be stored for later
visual.caption: A computer takes in, works on, shows and keeps data.

slides.narration: At its simplest, a computer is a machine with four jobs. It takes in data and instructions, processes them using the CPU, produces results, and can store both data and results for later. Keyboards, scanners and microphones are input; screens and printers are output; the CPU in the middle does the work.

visual.caption: Input, CPU, memory and output.

slides.narration: Here is the whole system at a glance. Input devices send data into the CPU. The CPU contains the control unit, the A L U and registers. It exchanges data with primary memory, which in turn is backed by secondary storage. Results go out to output devices. Notice that the CPU talks to memory in both directions.

slides.heading: Inside the CPU
slides.body_md: The **CPU** is the brain of the computer; its three working parts cooperate on every instruction.

rows: Adds, subtracts, compares, and performs AND, OR, NOT
Fetches an instruction, decodes it, directs the other parts
Tiny, very fast stores for the values being used right now

visual.alt: Table of the CPU parts: the ALU does arithmetic and logic, the control unit fetches, decodes and directs, and registers hold the values in use

slides.narration: The C P U has three working parts. The arithmetic logic unit, or A L U, performs calculations and logical comparisons. The control unit fetches each instruction from memory, decodes it and tells the other parts what to do. Registers are tiny, very fast stores that hold the values being worked on at this moment.

slides.heading: Quick check: who directs the work?
slides.body_md: Which unit fetches and decodes instructions?
slides.narration: Think about which part acts like the manager, not the calculator.

visual.caption: Wider bars hold more but are slower.

slides.narration: Memory comes in levels. At the top, registers are the fastest and the smallest. Cache comes next, then RAM, and at the bottom secondary storage, the slowest but the largest and cheapest per byte. A computer uses all four together, so that speed is available where it matters and capacity is available where it is needed.

slides.heading: Primary and secondary memory
slides.body_md: **Volatile** memory loses its contents when power is off; **non-volatile** memory keeps them.

rows: Keeps recently used data next to the CPU
Holds programs and data that are running
Holds start-up (boot) instructions; normally only read

visual.alt: Table of memory types: cache and RAM are volatile and hold data in use, ROM and secondary storage are non-volatile and hold start-up instructions and files

slides.narration: Cache and RAM are volatile. They hold what is running right now and are wiped when the power goes. ROM is non-volatile and holds the start-up instructions that boot the computer. Secondary storage such as an S S D or hard disk is also non-volatile and keeps your files. This is why unsaved work is lost in a power cut.

slides.heading: Measuring memory
slides.body_md: A **bit** is one binary digit; a **byte** is 8 bits. In this chapter **1 KB = 1024 bytes** and each larger unit is 1024 times the previous one.

visual.alt: Table of memory units: a bit is one binary digit, a nibble is 4 bits, a byte is 8 bits, and each of KB, MB, GB, TB and PB is 1024 times the one before it
visual.caption: Convention used here: 1 KB = 1024 bytes.

slides.narration: The smallest unit is the bit, a single zero or one. Four bits make a nibble and eight bits make a byte. A kilobyte is 1024 bytes, and every larger unit, megabyte, gigabyte, terabyte and petabyte, is 1024 times the one before it. We use 1024 throughout this chapter, as the syllabus does.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: converting units
slides.body_md: Larger unit to smaller: **multiply** by 1024. Smaller to larger: **divide** by 1024.
bullets: Step 1 — Decide which way you are going.
Step 2 — Multiply or divide by 1024 once for each step.
Step 3 — For a count of items, divide the total space by the size of one item.

rows: 4 MB songs on an 8 GB card

visual.alt: Worked example table of memory conversions: 3 GB is 3072 MB and 3145728 KB, 20480 KB is 20 MB, and an 8 GB card holds 2048 songs of 4 MB each
visual.caption: Larger unit to smaller: multiply. Smaller to larger: divide.

slides.narration: Going from a larger unit to a smaller one means multiplying. Three gigabytes is three times 1024, or 3072 megabytes, and multiplying by 1024 again gives 3145728 kilobytes. Going the other way, divide: 20480 kilobytes is 20 megabytes. An eight gigabyte card holds 2048 songs of four megabytes each.

slides.heading: Quick check: megabytes to kilobytes
slides.body_md: Try one yourself.
slides.narration: Remember to multiply when you move to a smaller unit, and use 1024 for each step.

slides.heading: Types of software
slides.body_md: **Software** is the set of programs that makes the hardware useful. There are three broad types, plus the translators that convert programs.

rows: Controls the hardware and runs other software
Maintains, protects and tunes the computer
Antivirus, backup, file compression, disk clean-up
Word processor, spreadsheet, a school fee program

visual.alt: Table of software types: system software controls hardware, utility software maintains and protects, application software helps users with tasks, and language translators convert programs into machine code

slides.narration: Software falls into three types. System software controls the hardware and runs other software; the operating system and device drivers belong here. Utility software maintains and protects the computer, for example an antivirus or a file compression tool. Application software helps users with tasks such as writing or accounting. Language translators convert programs into machine code.

slides.heading: Language translators
slides.body_md: A computer understands only **machine code**. Translators convert human-readable programs into it.

rows: Whole program at once; makes a separate executable
One statement at a time, then runs it

visual.alt: Table of language translators: an assembler converts assembly language, a compiler converts a whole high-level program into an executable, and an interpreter translates and runs one statement at a time and stops at the first error

slides.narration: A computer can run only machine code, so programs written by people must be translated. An assembler converts assembly language. A compiler translates a whole high-level program at once and lists all its errors together. An interpreter translates and runs one statement at a time, so it stops at the first error it meets.

slides.heading: Quick check: compiler or interpreter?
slides.body_md: True or false?
slides.narration: Think about which translator works on the whole program before anything runs.

slides.heading: Functions of an operating system
slides.body_md: The **operating system (OS)** manages the hardware and gives programs a base to run on.

rows: Music plays while you edit a document
Gives RAM to programs and takes it back
Closing an app frees its memory
Sending a page to the printer
Passwords, permissions, the screen you use

visual.alt: Table of operating system functions: process management shares the CPU, memory management allocates RAM, file management organises files, device management controls hardware through drivers, and security and the user interface protect and present the system

slides.narration: The operating system is the manager of the computer. It shares the CPU among running programs, which is process management. It allocates and recovers RAM, organises files in folders, and controls devices through drivers. It also provides security through passwords and permissions, and the screen you interact with, called the user interface.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: which kind of software?
slides.body_md: Ask: does it **run the machine**, **look after the machine**, **do a user task**, or **translate code**?
bullets: Step 1 — Read what the program does.
Step 2 — Match it to a type.
Step 3 — Say why in one phrase.

rows: Typing a letter in a word processor
Helps a user do a task
Zipping a folder to make it smaller
Lets the OS control one device
Converts assembly code to machine code

visual.alt: Worked example table: a word processor is application software, a file-zipping tool is utility software, a printer driver is system software, and an assembler is a language translator

slides.narration: To classify software, ask what it does. A word processor helps a person do a task, so it is application software. A tool that zips a folder tunes and maintains files, so it is a utility. A printer driver lets the operating system control one device, so it is system software. An assembler converts assembly code to machine code, so it is a translator.

slides.heading: Quick check: match the software
slides.body_md: Match each item with its kind of software.
slides.narration: Use the same questions: does it run, maintain, serve one customer or translate?

slides.heading: Summary

rows: ALU calculates, CU directs, registers hold values
Cache and RAM are volatile; ROM and secondary storage are not
1 KB = 1024 bytes; each unit is 1024 times the one before; 1 byte = 8 bits
System, utility, application; translators convert programs
Process, memory, file and device management, security and user interface

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: the CPU, memory types, memory units, software types and operating system functions

slides.narration: To sum up. The ALU calculates, the control unit directs and registers hold values. Cache and RAM are volatile, ROM and secondary storage are not. One kilobyte is 1024 bytes and each unit is 1024 times the one before. Software is system, utility or application, with translators in between, and the operating system manages processes, memory, files and devices.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: For unit questions, write the step: **multiply** going down, **divide** going up, with **1024** each time.
Say **volatile** or **non-volatile** whenever you compare memories.
Compiler: **whole program**; interpreter: **one statement at a time**.
Name the OS function and give a one-line example for each.
Match software to a type by **what it does**, not by its brand.
slides.narration: In the exam, show the multiply or divide step in unit questions and use 1024 every time. Always say whether a memory is volatile. For translators, remember whole program versus one statement at a time. For operating system functions, name the function and add an example. And classify software by what it does, not by who made it.

slides.heading: Logic, Numbers and Codes
slides.body_md: Part 2: how computers decide with **logic gates**, count with **binary** and store text with **encodings**.

slides.narration: Inside a computer everything is a pattern of zeros and ones. In this part we meet the logic gates that combine those bits, learn the laws of Boolean algebra, practise converting numbers between binary, octal, decimal and hexadecimal, and see how letters of every language are turned into codes.

slides.narration: A logic gate takes one or two input bits and produces one output bit. The NOT gate inverts its input. The AND gate gives one only when all inputs are one. The OR gate gives one when at least one input is one. NAND and NOR are AND and OR followed by NOT, shown with a small circle. XOR gives one only when its inputs differ.

slides.heading: Truth tables of the gates

visual.alt: Truth table of the five two-input gates: AND gives 0001, OR gives 0111, NAND gives 1110, NOR gives 1000 and XOR gives 0110 for the inputs 00, 01, 10 and 11
visual.caption: NOT: `0` gives 1, `1` gives 0.

slides.narration: A truth table lists every possible input and the output. For two inputs there are four rows. AND is one only in the last row. OR is zero only in the first. NAND is the opposite of AND, and NOR is the opposite of OR. XOR is one in the two middle rows, where the inputs differ.

slides.heading: Quick check: exactly one switch
slides.body_md: Which gate fits the hostel corridor lamp?
slides.narration: The lamp is on only when the two switches are in different positions.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a truth table
slides.body_md: Build the table for **F = (A AND B) OR (NOT C)**. Three inputs give 2 × 2 × 2 = **8 rows**.
bullets: Step 1 — List all combinations of A, B and C.
Step 2 — Work out A AND B and NOT C in their own columns.
Step 3 — OR the two columns to get F.

visual.alt: Worked example truth table of F equals (A AND B) OR (NOT C) with eight rows; F is 1 in 5 of them
visual.caption: F is 1 in 5 of the 8 rows.

slides.narration: Three inputs mean eight rows. First list every combination of A, B and C. Then work out the two smaller parts in their own columns: A AND B, and NOT C. Finally combine them with OR to get F. Counting the ones in the last column shows that F is one in 5 of the eight rows.

visual.caption: F = (A AND B) OR (NOT C).

slides.narration: Here is the same expression drawn as a circuit. Inputs A and B go into an AND gate. Input C goes into a NOT gate. The outputs of those two gates meet at an OR gate, whose output is F. Reading a circuit from left to right gives the order in which the expression is evaluated.

slides.heading: Boolean laws
slides.body_md: Laws let us **simplify** an expression and so build a circuit with fewer gates.

rows: A AND 1 = A;  A OR 0 = A
A AND A = A;  A OR A = A
A AND NOT A = 0;  A OR NOT A = 1
A AND B = B AND A;  A OR B = B OR A
(A AND B) AND C = A AND (B AND C);  likewise for OR
A AND (B OR C) = (A AND B) OR (A AND C);  A OR (B AND C) = (A OR B) AND (A OR C)
A OR (A AND B) = A;  A AND (A OR B) = A
NOT (A AND B) = (NOT A) OR (NOT B);  NOT (A OR B) = (NOT A) AND (NOT B)

visual.alt: Table of Boolean laws: identity, null, idempotent, complement, involution, commutative, associative, distributive, absorption and De Morgan
visual.caption: Some books write AND as a dot, OR as a plus and NOT as a bar or dash; this chapter uses the words.

slides.narration: Boolean algebra has laws, just like ordinary algebra. Identity and null laws involve zero and one. The complement law says a value and its opposite give zero with AND and one with OR. There are commutative, associative and distributive laws, the absorption law, and the two De Morgan laws on the next slide. Each can be checked with a truth table.

slides.heading: De Morgan's laws
slides.body_md: The complement of an **AND** is the **OR** of the complements; the complement of an **OR** is the **AND** of the complements.

visual.alt: Truth table verifying De Morgan's laws: NOT (A OR B) matches (NOT A) AND (NOT B) with 1000, and NOT (A AND B) matches (NOT A) OR (NOT B) with 1110
visual.caption: Equal columns prove each law.

slides.narration: De Morgan's laws connect AND and OR through NOT. NOT of A AND B equals NOT A OR NOT B. NOT of A OR B equals NOT A AND NOT B. In practice, break the bar, change the operator, and complement each term. The table confirms both laws, because each pair of columns is identical in all four rows.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: simplifying
slides.body_md: Simplify **(A AND B) OR (A AND NOT B)**, naming the law at each step.
bullets: Step 1 — Spot the common factor A.
Step 2 — Take it out with the distributive law.
Step 3 — Use the complement and identity laws.

rows: (A AND B) OR (A AND NOT B)

visual.alt: Worked example: (A AND B) OR (A AND NOT B) simplifies in four steps by the distributive, complement and identity laws to A; its truth table output 0011 matches A
visual.caption: A truth table agrees: the output column 0011 is the A column.

slides.narration: Look for a common factor. Both terms contain A, so the distributive law gives A AND, bracket, B OR NOT B. By the complement law, B OR NOT B is one. Then A AND one is A by the identity law. So a circuit with three gates reduces to a plain wire. A truth table confirms the result.

slides.heading: Quick check: De Morgan's law
slides.body_md: True or false?
slides.narration: Try the inputs one and zero on both sides.

slides.heading: Number systems
slides.body_md: A system of **base b** uses b digits. Binary is base **2**, octal **8**, decimal **10** and hexadecimal **16**.
bullets: Binary: digits 0 and 1.
Octal: digits 0 to 7.
Hexadecimal: digits 0 to 9 and A to F (A is 10, F is 15).

visual.alt: Table of the numbers 0 to 15 in decimal, 4-bit binary, octal and hexadecimal; the hexadecimal digits A to F stand for 10 to 15
visual.caption: Hex digits: A=10, B=11, C=12, D=13, E=14, F=15.

slides.narration: Computers use binary, base two, with only the digits zero and one. Octal is base eight and hexadecimal is base sixteen, which needs letters A to F for the values ten to fifteen. Each octal digit stands for three bits and each hexadecimal digit for four bits, which makes them handy short forms for long binary numbers.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: decimal to binary
slides.body_md: Divide by 2 again and again; the **remainders**, read from the **bottom up**, are the binary number.
bullets: Check with Python: `bin(45)` gives `0b101101`, where 0b only marks a binary literal.

visual.alt: Worked example: repeated division of 45 by 2 gives remainders that read upward as 101101
visual.caption: Read the remainders from the bottom up: 101101.

slides.narration: Take forty-five. Divide by two, and note the quotient and remainder. Keep dividing the quotient until it reaches zero. The remainders, read from the last to the first, give the binary number 101101. A quick check with place values, thirty-two plus eight plus four plus one, gives forty-five again.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: grouping bits
slides.body_md: Binary to **octal**: groups of **3** bits. Binary to **hexadecimal**: groups of **4** bits. Start grouping from the **right**.
bullets: Pad the left end with zeros to complete the last group.
Hexadecimal to binary: replace each digit by its 4 bits.

visual.alt: Worked example table: binary 1011100110 is octal 1346 and hexadecimal 2E6; hexadecimal 3AF is binary 1110101111; binary 110101 is decimal 53
visual.caption: Pad with leading zeros to complete the first group.

slides.narration: Because eight is two cubed and sixteen is two to the fourth, binary converts to octal and hexadecimal by grouping. Group bits in threes for octal and in fours for hexadecimal, starting from the right and padding on the left with zeros. To go back, replace each hexadecimal digit by its four bits. Binary to decimal is just adding the place values.

slides.heading: Quick check: hexadecimal to decimal
slides.body_md: Convert with place values.
slides.narration: The left digit is worth sixteen times its face value. The letter C is worth twelve.

slides.heading: Fractions in binary
slides.body_md: Whole part: **divide** by 2. Fraction part: **multiply** by 2 and collect the whole-number bits.

visual.alt: Worked example: 13.75 is 1101 for the whole part, and multiplying 0.75 by 2 repeatedly gives the bits 1 and 1, so the binary number is 1101.11; binary 110.011 is 6.375 in decimal
visual.caption: Whole part: divide by 2. Fraction part: multiply by 2.

slides.narration: Fractions need a second method. Convert the whole part by repeated division. For the fraction, multiply by two, write down the whole number part, which is the next bit, and repeat with what is left until it reaches zero. Thirteen point seven five becomes 1101 point 11. To go back, binary places after the point are halves, quarters and eighths.

slides.heading: ASCII, ISCII and Unicode
slides.body_md: An **encoding** gives each character a **code**. Older schemes were small; **Unicode** gives every character of every script a unique **code point**.

rows: English letters, digits, punctuation, control codes
ASCII in the lower half; Indian scripts in the upper half

visual.alt: Table comparing ASCII with 7 bits and 128 codes, extended ASCII and ISCII with 8 bits and 256 codes, and Unicode with 1114112 possible code points covering every script
visual.caption: Unicode includes ASCII unchanged as its first 128 code points.

slides.narration: An encoding assigns a number to each character. ASCII uses seven bits, which gives 128 codes for English. Extended ASCII and ISCII use eight bits. ISCII keeps ASCII in its lower half and uses the upper half for Indian scripts. Unicode ends the clash between schemes by giving every character of every script its own code point, with ASCII as its first 128.

slides.heading: UTF-8 and UTF-32
slides.body_md: **UTF-8** stores a code point in **1 to 4 bytes**; **UTF-32** always uses **4 bytes**.

visual.alt: Table of UTF-8 lengths: code points up to U+007F take 1 byte, up to U+07FF take 2 bytes, up to U+FFFF take 3 bytes, and above that 4 bytes; UTF-32 always uses 4 bytes
visual.caption: UTF-32 always uses 4 bytes per character.

slides.narration: A code point still has to be stored as bytes, and that is what UTF encodings do. UTF-8 uses between one and four bytes. English letters take just one, which keeps old ASCII text unchanged, and other characters take two, three or four. UTF-32 is simpler but wasteful, since every character takes exactly four bytes.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: bytes of real characters
slides.body_md: Python can show the exact bytes: `'₹'.encode('utf-8')` gives `b'\xe2\x82\xb9'`.
bullets: Step 1 — Find the code point.
Step 2 — Match it to a range to get the UTF-8 length.
Step 3 — UTF-32 is always 4 bytes.

visual.alt: Table of real characters with their Unicode code point, UTF-8 bytes in hexadecimal, byte count, and 4-byte UTF-32 code; A takes 1 byte, é takes 2, the Devanagari letter ka takes 3, the rupee sign takes 3 and an emoji takes 4 bytes in UTF-8
visual.caption: Computed with Python: `ch.encode('utf-8')`.

slides.narration: The letter A has code point forty-one in hexadecimal and takes one byte in UTF-8. The letter e with an acute accent takes two bytes. The Hindi letter ka and the rupee sign each take three bytes. An emoji takes four. In UTF-32 every one of them takes exactly four bytes.

slides.heading: Quick check: the rupee sign
slides.body_md: How many bytes in UTF-8?
slides.narration: Find which range the code point falls in.

slides.heading: Summary

rows: AND all 1; OR any 1; NOT inverts; NAND, NOR invert AND, OR; XOR needs inputs to differ
2 to the power of the inputs rows; evaluate NOT, then AND, then OR
De Morgan: change AND to OR (or back) and complement each term
Divide for whole parts, multiply for fractions, group bits in 3s or 4s
ASCII 7 bits, ISCII 8 bits, Unicode one code point each; UTF-8 1 to 4 bytes, UTF-32 4 bytes

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: gates, truth tables, Boolean laws, number conversions and character encodings

slides.narration: To sum up. AND needs all ones, OR needs one, NOT inverts, and XOR needs different inputs. A truth table has two to the power of the inputs rows. De Morgan: change the operator and complement each term. Divide for whole parts, multiply for fractions, and group bits in threes or fours. ASCII has seven bits, ISCII eight, and Unicode one code point per character.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Rows in a truth table = **2 to the power of the number of inputs**.
Evaluate in order: **NOT, then AND, then OR**; use brackets to be safe.
Name the **law** next to each simplification step.
Show the **division table** for conversions; group from the **right**.
Say **how many bytes** and **why** when comparing UTF-8 and UTF-32.
slides.narration: Remember that a truth table has two to the power of the inputs rows. Evaluate NOT first, then AND, then OR. When you simplify, name the law beside each step. For conversions, show the division table and group bits from the right. And for encodings, give the byte counts and the reason for the difference between UTF-8 and UTF-32.

sections.heading: 1. Computer organisation, memory and units
sections.body_md:
A computer **accepts input**, **processes** it, gives **output** and **stores** data. Its parts: **input devices**, the **CPU**, **memory** and **output devices**.

**CPU:** the **ALU** does arithmetic and logic; the **control unit** fetches, decodes and directs; **registers** hold the values in use.

**Memory:** **registers** (fastest) then **cache**, **RAM**, **secondary storage** (slowest, largest). **Cache** and **RAM** are **volatile**; **ROM** (boot instructions) and **secondary storage** (files) are **non-volatile**.

**Units:** 1 byte = 8 bits; a **nibble** is 4 bits. We use **1 KB = 1024 bytes**, 1 MB = 1024 KB, 1 GB = 1024 MB, 1 TB = 1024 GB, 1 PB = 1024 TB. Larger to smaller: **multiply**; smaller to larger: **divide**.

Small, very fast memory that keeps recently used data close to the CPU.

sections.heading: 2. Software and the operating system
sections.body_md:
**System software** controls the hardware and runs other software: the **operating system** and **device drivers**. **Utility software** maintains and protects the computer: antivirus, backup, file compression, disk clean-up. **Application software** helps with user tasks: **general-purpose** (word processor, spreadsheet), **specific-purpose** (a billing or booking package) or **custom** (written for one user).

**Translators:** an **assembler** converts assembly language; a **compiler** translates the whole program and lists all errors; an **interpreter** translates and runs one statement at a time and stops at the first error.

**OS functions:** process management, memory management, file management, device management, security and the user interface.

sections.heading: 3. Logic gates and truth tables
sections.body_md:
**Boolean values** are 0 and 1. **NOT** inverts a single bit. **AND** gives 1 only when **all** inputs are 1. **OR** gives 1 when **at least one** input is 1. **NAND** is NOT of AND; **NOR** is NOT of OR; **XOR** gives 1 only when the two inputs **differ**.

A **truth table** lists every input combination and the output; n inputs give **2 to the power n** rows. Evaluate in the order **NOT, AND, OR**.

**Universal gates:** NAND and NOR. Tying both NAND inputs together gives a NOT gate.

key_terms.definition_md: A table that lists the output of a Boolean expression for every input combination.
A gate from which every other gate can be built; NAND and NOR are universal.

sections.heading: 4. Boolean laws and De Morgan
sections.body_md:
Laws: **identity, null, idempotent, complement, involution, commutative, associative, distributive** and **absorption** (see the table). **De Morgan's laws:** NOT (A AND B) = (NOT A) OR (NOT B); NOT (A OR B) = (NOT A) AND (NOT B). The rule: break the bar, change AND to OR (or OR to AND), complement each term.

**Simplifying** an expression reduces the gates in a circuit; name the law at each step. Two expressions are equal if their **truth tables are identical**.

key_terms.definition_md: Rules that turn the complement of an AND into an OR of complements, and the complement of an OR into an AND of complements.

A AND B = B AND A;  A OR B = B OR A

A AND (B OR C) = (A AND B) OR (A AND C);  A OR (B AND C) = (A OR B) AND (A OR C)
A OR (A AND B) = A;  A AND (A OR B) = A
NOT (A AND B) = (NOT A) OR (NOT B);  NOT (A OR B) = (NOT A) AND (NOT B)

sections.heading: 5. Number systems and conversions
sections.body_md:
**Binary** (base 2): 0, 1. **Octal** (base 8): 0 to 7. **Decimal** (base 10). **Hexadecimal** (base 16): 0 to 9 and A to F (A = 10 … F = 15).

- **Decimal to binary:** divide by 2 repeatedly, read the **remainders upward**.
- **Binary to decimal:** add the place values of the 1 bits (…, 8, 4, 2, 1).
- **Binary to octal / hex:** group bits in **3** / **4** from the **right**, padding with zeros on the left.
- **Octal / hex to binary:** replace each digit with 3 / 4 bits.
- **Fractions:** whole part by division; fraction part by **multiplying by 2** and collecting the whole-number bits. Binary places after the point are halves, quarters, eighths.

sections.heading: 6. Encoding schemes
sections.body_md:
An **encoding** assigns a code to every character. **ASCII**: 7 bits, 128 codes, English only (A is 65, a is 97, 0 is 48; small and capital letters differ by 32). **Extended ASCII** and **ISCII**: 8 bits; ISCII keeps ASCII in the lower half and covers **Indian scripts** above it. **Unicode**: a unique **code point** for every character of every script; its first 128 are ASCII.

**UTF-8:** 1 to 4 bytes per character (English letters take 1, so ASCII text is unchanged). **UTF-32:** always 4 bytes. A text with many English letters is smaller in UTF-8; UTF-32 is simpler but uses more space.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Using 1000 instead of **1024** for a step between memory units, or dividing when you should multiply.
- Calling RAM non-volatile, or ROM volatile.
- Writing the remainders of a division **top down** instead of bottom up.
- Grouping bits from the **left** instead of the right when converting to octal or hexadecimal.
- Writing NOT (A AND B) = (NOT A) AND (NOT B): the operator must **change** to OR.
- Forgetting that a hexadecimal digit stands for **exactly 4 bits** (and an octal digit for 3).
- Saying UTF-8 always uses 1 byte, or UTF-32 a variable number of bytes.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: one fact or one correct choice.
- 2 to 3 marks: the answer **plus a reason**, or a conversion with its working.
- 4 marks (case-based): small parts, each short, with a choice in the last part.
- 5 marks: a full answer in ordered points, a complete truth table or a series of conversions with working.

questions.stem_md: Inside the processor of Tara's school computer, which unit fetches each instruction from memory, decodes it and tells the other parts what to do next?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Control unit. The control unit runs the fetch, decode and execute steps and directs the other parts. The ALU only calculates and compares, cache is fast memory, and an output unit is not inside the CPU.

questions.stem_md: Gopal was typing his Hindi essay when the lab lost power before he pressed Save. Which memory was holding the unsaved text, so that it vanished?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** RAM. Work that is open but unsaved lives in RAM, which is volatile and empties when power fails. The hard disk and pen drive are non-volatile secondary storage; ROM holds fixed start-up instructions.

questions.stem_md: Taking 1 KB = 1024 bytes and 1 MB = 1024 KB, a slide deck of 3 MB is how many KB?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 3072 KB. Multiply by 1024 to go from MB to KB: 3 × 1024 = 3072. The round figure 3000 uses a step of 1000, which this chapter does not use.

questions.stem_md: A plain-text file of Naveen's diary entries is 2 KB (1 KB = 1024 bytes). How many bits does it hold?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 16384 bits. First change KB to bytes: 2 × 1024 = 2048 bytes. Each byte has 8 bits, so 2048 × 8 = 16384 bits. 2048 is the byte count, not the bit count.

questions.stem_md: Fatima's empty pen drive holds 16 GB. Every phone photo she copies is 2 MB. Taking 1 GB = 1024 MB, how many such photos fit on it?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 8192. 16 GB = 16 × 1024 = 16384 MB, and 16384 ÷ 2 = 8192 photos. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 32768.

questions.stem_md: Dev's script prints the results of lines 1 to 6 and then stops with an error message at line 7, without running anything after it. Which language translator is processing his script?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Interpreter. An interpreter translates and runs one statement at a time, so the first six lines had already executed when line 7 failed. A compiler reports its errors before any of the program runs.

questions.stem_md: After Kavita plugged a new label printer into her shop computer, it did nothing until she installed a small program supplied by its maker. What is that program?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Device driver. A device driver lets the operating system control a particular piece of hardware. The other options do not give the system knowledge of a new device.

questions.stem_md: Each Sunday the lab of an imagined school in Mysuru runs a program that scans every drive for malicious files and quarantines them. This program is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** utility software. Utility software maintains and protects the computer; an antivirus scanner is a standard example. It does not translate programs, serve one customer's business needs, or sit in ROM.

questions.stem_md: Ishaan renames a folder, moves a document into it and deletes an old copy. Which function of the operating system carries out these operations?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** File management. Creating, naming, moving and deleting files and folders is file management. Process management shares the CPU, memory management allocates RAM, and device management controls hardware.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Whatever is stored in RAM stays intact after the computer is switched off.
questions.solution_md: **False.** RAM is volatile: it loses its contents without power. Non-volatile memory such as ROM or an SSD keeps data.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A compiler translates the whole source program into machine code before the program is run.
questions.solution_md: **True.** A compiler translates the complete program in one pass and produces a separate executable file, unlike an interpreter that works statement by statement.

questions.stem_md: The CPU has an ___ unit that carries out calculations and comparisons, and a ___ unit that directs the other components.
questions.solution_md: The arithmetic logic unit (ALU) calculates and compares; the control unit (CU) directs the operation of the other components.

questions.stem_md: One byte is made up of ___ bits, and in this chapter 1 KB equals ___ bytes.
questions.solution_md: A byte has 8 bits, and the syllabus convention for a kilobyte is 1024 bytes.

questions.stem_md: Name the two main parts of the CPU and state one job of each.
questions.solution_md: ALU with its job, control unit with its job.

answer.model_answer_md: The **arithmetic logic unit (ALU)** performs arithmetic operations and logical comparisons. The **control unit (CU)** fetches and decodes instructions and directs the other components to carry them out.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between RAM and ROM on any two points.
questions.solution_md: Two valid differences: volatility, and use or read-write nature.

answer.model_answer_md: **RAM** is volatile and loses its contents without power; it is read-write memory holding running programs and data. **ROM** is non-volatile and keeps its contents; it holds fixed start-up (boot) instructions and is normally only read.

questions.stem_md: How does a compiler differ from an interpreter in the way it translates a program?
questions.solution_md: Whole program versus statement by statement, with the error behaviour.

answer.model_answer_md: A **compiler** translates the whole program into machine code first and lists all its errors together; the result runs without the compiler. An **interpreter** translates and executes one statement at a time and stops at the first error it meets.

questions.stem_md: State any two functions of an operating system and give an everyday example of each.
questions.solution_md: Any two functions, each with a fitting example.

answer.model_answer_md: **Process management** shares the CPU among running programs, for example playing music while a document is edited. **File management** organises files in folders, for example creating, renaming or deleting a file.

questions.stem_md: Classify software into system, utility and application software, with one example of each.
questions.solution_md: Each of the three classes with its role and one example.

answer.model_answer_md: **System software** controls the hardware and runs other software, e.g. an operating system or a device driver. **Utility software** maintains and protects the computer, e.g. an antivirus scanner or a disk-cleanup tool. **Application software** helps users do a task, e.g. a word processor, a spreadsheet or a school fee program.

questions.stem_md: A computer has registers, cache, RAM and a hard disk. Why not build all of its storage from the fastest type?
questions.solution_md: Cost and size against speed, and the role of permanent storage.

answer.model_answer_md: The fastest memory (registers, cache) is very **costly** per byte and can only be made small. The slowest (hard disk) is cheap and large and keeps data **permanently**. A hierarchy gives speed where it matters, capacity at low cost, and non-volatile storage for files.

marking_scheme.step: Fast memory costs more and is small
Slow memory is cheap, large and permanent

questions.stem_md: Describe the organisation of a computer system. Cover input devices, the CPU and its parts, primary memory, secondary memory and output devices, and say how data moves between them.
questions.solution_md: Five parts with correct roles and the direction of data flow.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Input devices** (keyboard, scanner) take data into the computer.
2. The **CPU** processes it: the **control unit** fetches and decodes instructions, the **ALU** calculates and compares, and **registers** hold values being used right now.
3. **Primary memory** (RAM, ROM, cache) is directly reachable by the CPU; RAM is volatile and holds running programs.
4. **Secondary memory** (hard disk, SSD) keeps programs and files permanently.
5. **Output devices** (monitor, printer) show the result. Data flows input, memory, CPU, memory, output.

questions.stem_md: Dr Anjali opens a small eye clinic in Coimbatore with two computers. She needs patient records and bills, protection from malicious files, a programmer to write a booking tool in Python, and a system that runs it all. Name the kind of software for each need and justify one choice in a sentence.
questions.solution_md: Four needs matched to application, utility, translator and system software, with one justification.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Patient records and bills: **application software**, ideally custom or a ready billing package.
